chunks: "There isn't one motor temperature; there are several, each tied to a different failure.
The most important is the winding, since the copper is where the heat is made and the insulation is what dies.
I care about the hot spot, but I can usually only measure the average, through a sensor embedded in the end turns or by looking at winding resistance.
Then the stator core and the housing, which lag the winding but are easy to measure and tell you about cooling and ambient.
In a permanent-magnet motor the rotor and magnets matter too. Neodymium magnets lose strength as they heat, about 0.
1 percent per kelvin of flux, and they can partly demagnetise if they get too hot, but the rotor spins, so you can't put a sensor on it.
You estimate it from a model, or from the back-EMF constant, or use IR or telemetry in test.
Bearings: grease has a temperature limit, and bearing temperature rising relative to the housing is a sign of wear. In brushed motors, the commutator and brushes run hot and wear.
Finally the electronics: the MOSFET junction, the shunt and the board.
I can't measure the junction directly, but I can compute it from power loss and thermal resistance, or measure the case or an NTC on the board and add a margin.
Which ones I can measure directly: anything stationary and reachable. Rotating parts need IR, slip rings or estimation."
